stem: Corporate strategy is primarily concerned with…

options.text: Where the firm competes: which industries and markets it is in
How the firm competes within a single industry
options.why: That is business strategy.

options.text: Short-term actions that implement a plan
options.why: Those are tactics.
Values describe how the organisation behaves, not the scope of its businesses.

explanation: Corporate strategy = WHERE to compete (the business portfolio, linked to industry attractiveness); business strategy = HOW to compete (competitive advantage).

stem: Which is NOT one of Grant's four elements of a successful strategy?

options.why: This is one of the four elements.

options.text: Profound understanding of the competitive environment
options.why: This is one of the four elements.
This is one of the four elements.

explanation: The four elements are goals, understanding of the environment, objective appraisal of resources and effective implementation.
source: S1 · Four elements of a successful strategy

stem: The vision describes why the organisation exists today; the mission describes what it wants to become.
explanation: It is the other way round: the mission is the present purpose (why we exist), the vision is the future (what we want to become).

stem: Strategy as 'positioning' answers which questions?

options.text: Where are we competing and how are we competing?
What do we want to become and how will we get there?
options.why: These are strategy as direction (preparing for the future).
That is about corporate identity, not positioning.

options.text: Which tactics should we use this quarter?
options.why: Tactics are short-term actions, not strategy.

explanation: Positioning = competing for the present (where and how); direction = preparing for the future.

stem: In the Ansoff matrix, selling an existing product in a new geographical market is…

options.why: Penetration = existing product, existing market.
Product development = new product, existing market.
Diversification = new product AND new market.

explanation: Market development = existing product × new market.

stem: According to Porter, an industry is most attractive when…

options.text: The five competitive forces are weak
The five competitive forces are strong
options.why: Strong forces squeeze profits and make the industry unattractive.
Substitutes cap prices and lower attractiveness.
Concentrated buyers have more bargaining power, reducing profitability.

explanation: Strong forces → low attractiveness → low profitability. Weak forces leave more profit potential.

stem: Which factor INCREASES rivalry among existing competitors?

options.why: Differentiation reduces price competition.
Growth lets firms expand without stealing share; slow growth intensifies rivalry.
High (not low) fixed costs push firms to cut prices to fill capacity.

explanation: High exit barriers keep unprofitable firms in the market, adding excess capacity and price competition.

stem: Complements are one of Porter's original five forces.
explanation: Complements are a 'missing factor' in the Five Forces (sometimes called a sixth force). A complement increases the value of another product; a substitute replaces it.

stem: The key criterion for defining an industry's boundaries is…

options.text: Substitutability on the demand and supply side

options.why: SIC codes can help, but boundaries depend on substitutability and the purpose of the analysis.

options.text: The number of firms in the market
options.why: That describes structure, not boundaries.
Mission is internal and does not define the industry.

explanation: Demand side: will customers switch? Supply side: can producers switch production? Boundaries also depend on the purpose of the analysis.

stem: Plant-based meat grew fast, yet pioneers like Beyond Meat struggled to make profits. The best Five Forces explanation is…

options.text: Low entry barriers, strong substitutes (conventional meat), powerful retail buyers and intense rivalry
Very high entry barriers protecting incumbents
options.why: Barriers were low: large food firms and private labels entered easily.
Retailers and fast-food chains are powerful buyers; conventional meat is a strong substitute.
Growth is not attractiveness; structure determines profitability.

explanation: High growth ≠ high attractiveness: weak structural protection squeezed profits despite innovation.

stem: A strategic group is…

options.text: A group of firms in an industry following the same or similar strategies
A group of customers with similar needs
options.why: That is a market segment.

options.text: A cross-functional team inside a firm
options.why: Not the strategy concept.

options.text: A coalition of firms lobbying the government
options.why: Coalitions are a defensive tactic (S19), not strategic groups.

explanation: Segments cluster customers; strategic groups cluster firms.

stem: Barriers that prevent firms from moving from one strategic group to another are called…

options.why: Exit barriers keep firms in the industry.
Switching costs apply to buyers changing supplier.
These are a source of entry barriers into the industry.

explanation: Mobility barriers are entry barriers within an industry, protecting a strategic group.

stem: Rivalry is usually most intense within a strategic group rather than between groups.
explanation: Firms in the same group follow similar strategies and target similar customers, so they are each other's closest competitors.

stem: What is the purpose of segmentation analysis in strategy?

options.text: To identify which parts of an industry are attractive and what it takes to succeed there

options.why: Mission is a corporate-identity question.

options.text: To measure the firm's cost position
options.why: That is value-chain cost analysis (S6).

options.text: To choose between licensing and joint ventures
options.why: That is an entry-mode decision (S12).

explanation: Industry analysis asks if the industry is attractive; segmentation asks which parts are; KSFs say what to do well there.

stem: MyStyleBags segmented its customers by usage occasion. Which set fits that variable?

options.why: That is gender, another variable mentioned.
That is geography.
That is income/price.

explanation: Usage occasion = what the bag is used for; personalisation then raised perceived value and lowered price sensitivity.

stem: In VRIO, a resource that is valuable but NOT rare gives…

options.why: Disadvantage = not valuable.
Temporary advantage needs valuable + rare (but imitable).
Sustained advantage requires all four: V, R, I, O.

explanation: Valuable + not rare = parity: useful, but competitors have it too.

stem: Valuable, rare and inimitable — but the firm is not organised to exploit it. VRIO outcome?

options.why: Needs the 'O' as well.
Parity is valuable but not rare.
Temporary = imitable.

explanation: Without organisation (processes, systems, structure) the potential advantage is not captured.

stem: Which statement best distinguishes resources from capabilities?

options.text: Resources are what the firm HAS; capabilities are what it CAN DO
Resources are intangible; capabilities are tangible
options.why: Resources can be tangible, intangible or human.

options.text: Capabilities appear on the balance sheet; resources do not
options.why: Many resources (brand, know-how) and all capabilities are off the balance sheet.
Grant distinguishes them clearly.

explanation: Example: skilled employees = resource; ability to develop products quickly = capability.

stem: A core competence (Prahalad & Hamel) must…

options.text: Contribute disproportionately to customer value or efficiency and provide a basis for entering new markets
Simply be something the firm does better than rivals
options.why: That is Selznick's distinctive competence.
Patents are one form of protection, not part of the definition.

options.text: Be located in the R&D function
options.why: Core competences are often cross-functional.

explanation: Example: Honda's engine competence spans motorcycles, cars, generators and marine engines.

stem: In class, Sweetgreen's digital ordering and delivery was rated a source of sustained competitive advantage.
explanation: Digital ordering is valuable but easy to imitate → competitive parity. Direct farmer relationships were the stronger candidate for sustained advantage.

stem: Economies of learning reduce unit costs as…

options.why: That is economies of scale.

options.text: The firm shares activities across products
options.why: That is economies of scope.
That is network economies — a demand-side effect.

explanation: Scale = current output; learning = cumulative output (experience curve, typically 20–30% per doubling).

stem: A firm with a cost advantage must charge lower prices than its competitors.
explanation: It can keep market prices and earn higher margins, or cut prices to gain share — cost advantage ≠ low price.

stem: Low-cost airlines operating a single aircraft type mainly exploit which cost driver?

options.text: Product design / standardisation (simpler training, maintenance, spares)

options.why: Not a cost driver; it's a demand-side effect.
Culture helps, but a single fleet is a design/standardisation choice.
This is a cost, not differentiation, strategy.

explanation: A standardised fleet simplifies training, maintenance and spare parts, and supports learning economies.

stem: What is the correct order of the five steps of value-chain cost analysis?

options.text: Identify activities → allocate costs → identify cost drivers → identify linkages → recommend reductions
Recommend reductions → identify activities → allocate costs → drivers → linkages
options.why: Recommendations come last.

options.text: Identify cost drivers → identify activities → recommend → allocate → linkages
options.why: Activities must be identified first.

options.text: Allocate costs → recommend → identify activities → linkages → drivers
options.why: Wrong order.

explanation: Linkages matter: cutting cost in one activity can raise costs elsewhere (e.g., cheaper parts → more defects).

stem: In the Southwest vs United comparison, Southwest had lower total cost despite higher maintenance cost. The lesson is that…

options.text: Cost advantage comes from an integrated system of reinforcing activities, not from being cheapest in every activity
Maintenance is irrelevant to airline costs
options.why: It is relevant — Southwest simply won overall.

options.text: United was stuck in the middle
options.why: The comparison illustrates system effects, not generic strategy failure.
Southwest was smaller; its advantage was the activity system.

explanation: A reinforcing system (unbundling, one fleet, secondary airports, fast turnaround) is also harder to imitate.

stem: Porter's cost focus strategy combines…

options.text: Lower cost with a broad market
options.why: That is cost leadership.

options.text: Lower cost with a narrow market segment

options.why: That is differentiation focus.
That is broad differentiation.

explanation: Generic strategies = source of advantage (cost vs differentiation) × scope (broad vs narrow). Example: Basko.

stem: Differentiation always requires segmentation.
explanation: Broad-scope differentiation appeals to needs many customers share (McDonald's, Honda, Gillette). Differentiation = how; segmentation = where.

stem: Signalling becomes MORE important for differentiation when…

options.text: Product quality is hard to judge before purchase (experience goods)
Product quality is easy to inspect before purchase
options.why: For search goods, buyers can check quality directly.

options.text: The firm is a cost leader
options.why: Signalling concerns perceived value, not cost position.
Commodities offer little to signal.

explanation: The harder it is to evaluate performance before buying, the more brand, packaging, premises and reputation matter.

stem: Which is a SUPPLY-side driver of uniqueness?

options.text: Customers' willingness to pay a premium
options.why: That is demand-side analysis.
Demand-side.
Demand-side.

explanation: The nine drivers of uniqueness (features, services, marketing, technology, inputs, procedures, skills, location, vertical integration) are supply-side.

stem: Chantecler's Campanella turns a local symbol into a recognisable luxury jewel. Which concepts explain its advantage best?

options.text: Intangible differentiation and signalling, supported by heritage that is hard to imitate (VRIO)
Cost leadership through economies of scale
options.why: Chantecler competes on uniqueness, not low cost.
Not relevant to jewellery value.
It has a clear differentiation-focus position.

explanation: Story, symbol and Capri heritage create intangible value; heritage is path-dependent and hard to imitate.
